title: Distal radius fracture: reading the X-ray and planning treatment

guidelineVersions: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (December 2017)

related.why: Same BOAST and NICE NG38 framework applied to the ankle

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in trauma and orthopaedics
brief.scenario: Mrs Margaret Cairns, 72, tripped on a rug and fell onto her outstretched left hand. Her wrist is swollen and deformed. She lives alone and is independent. Written findings: PA and lateral radiographs of the left wrist; the growth plates are fused. On the PA view there is a transverse fracture across the distal radius just above the wrist joint; the fracture line does not reach the joint surface. The radius is shortened, so the ulnar head projects 4 mm beyond the radial joint surface. There is a separate fracture through the ulnar styloid. On the lateral view the distal radial fragment is tilted so its joint surface faces 25 degrees towards the back of the hand, and the fragment is shifted backwards relative to the shaft.
brief.task: Interpret the written radiograph findings and discuss her management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Describe the fracture, check the median nerve, then decide by age, displacement and the joint.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Using a haematoma block by reflex, or plating every displaced fracture regardless of age.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "These are PA and lateral views of a left wrist in a skeletally mature patient."

grid.label: Describing the fracture
grid.fail: Says 'broken wrist', or calls a dorsally displaced fracture a Smith's.
grid.pass: Extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, dorsal displacement and radial shortening: a Colles-type fracture.
grid.high: Comments systematically on articular step, ulnar variance, dorsal tilt and ulnar styloid, the features that guide surgery.

grid.label: Neurovascular status and skin
grid.fail: Does not test the median nerve before or after manipulation.
grid.pass: Documents skin, circulation and median nerve sensation (index finger pulp) before and after manipulation.
grid.high: Recognises worsening median numbness after reduction as acute carpal tunnel syndrome needing urgent decompression.

grid.label: Anaesthesia for manipulation
grid.fail: Manipulates under gas and air alone, or uses a haematoma block by default.
grid.pass: Manipulates under regional anaesthesia, such as a Bier's block, by a trained practitioner.
grid.high: States BOAST prefers regional anaesthesia to a haematoma block and NICE advises against gas and air on its own.

grid.label: Cast and follow-up
grid.fail: Casts in forced palmar flexion, or omits a post-reduction X-ray.
grid.pass: Neutral wrist, three-point moulding, check X-ray; fracture clinic assessment within 72 hours.
grid.high: Repeat X-ray at 1 to 2 weeks if unstable and re-displacement would change management; consider cast removal at 4 weeks.

grid.label: Operate or not
grid.fail: Plates every displaced fracture regardless of age, or never considers surgery.
grid.pass: At 65 or over, non-operative treatment can be primary unless significant deformity or nerve compromise. Volar displaced fractures are unstable: consider plating.
grid.high: Under 65 weighs ulnar variance, articular step, dorsal tilt and demands. K-wires if the joint reduces closed; otherwise ORIF.

grid.label: Timing of surgery
grid.fail: Cannot give timings, or lets surgery drift.
grid.pass: Within 72 hours of injury for intra-articular fractures; within 7 days for extra-articular fractures.
grid.high: For re-displacement after manipulation, within 72 hours of the decision to operate.

grid.label: Bone health and recovery
grid.fail: Discharges her without considering falls or bone health.
grid.pass: Treats it as a fragility fracture: falls risk and bone health assessment, referral to the fracture liaison service.
grid.high: Warns of stiffness, malunion, CRPS and EPL rupture; advises on driving and function, and gives a self-referral route.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What else in the findings guides you?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Whether the joint is involved and by how much, ulnar variance, dorsal tilt, and the ulnar styloid. Those guide whether surgery would help.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After manipulation she says her index finger is going numb.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's acute carpal tunnel syndrome. I'd split the cast, elevate, and if it doesn't settle quickly she needs urgent carpal tunnel decompression.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: BOAST prefers regional anaesthesia to a haematoma block, and NICE advises against gas and air on its own.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If the pattern is unstable and re-displacement would change management, repeat X-rays at 1 to 2 weeks. Otherwise consider removing the cast at 4 weeks.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if she were 45 and a keen climber?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd weigh ulnar variance, articular step, dorsal tilt and her demands. If the joint reduces closed, K-wires; if not, open reduction and plating.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Operate within 72 hours of that decision.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd warn her about stiffness, malunion, CRPS and extensor pollicis longus rupture, advise on driving, and give her a way to self-refer.

failures.move: Not testing median nerve sensation before and after manipulation.
failures.consequence: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome is missed and permanent median nerve damage can follow.

failures.move: Reducing under gas and air alone.
failures.consequence: Poor analgesia gives a poor reduction; NICE advises against it.
Median nerve compression and a stiff wrist, without holding the fracture better.

failures.move: Offering a plate to every displaced fracture in an older patient.
failures.consequence: Surgical risk without functional gain; non-operative treatment is an accepted primary option at 65 or over.

recovery.line: Regional anaesthesia, such as a Bier's block, by someone trained in it; not gas and air alone.
It depends on age, displacement direction, the joint and her demands; at her age non-operative treatment is often right.

knowledge.fact: Manipulate under regional anaesthesia (for example Bier's block) rather than a haematoma block; never gas and air alone.
Cast: neutral wrist, three-point moulding; consider removal at 4 weeks.
At 65 or over, non-operative treatment can be primary for dorsally displaced fractures unless significant deformity or nerve compromise.
Volar displaced (Smith's) fractures are unstable: consider plating.
Surgery: intra-articular within 72 hours of injury; extra-articular within 7 days; re-displacement within 72 hours of decision.
K-wires if the joint reduces closed; ORIF if not.

recall.think: Median nerve compromise, skin, and a fragility fracture.
do: Document skin and median nerve before and after
Reduce under regional anaesthesia; neutral cast, three-point mould
recall.trap: A good-looking X-ray does not mean the median nerve is safe.
recall.finish: Cast if acceptable for her needs; K-wires or ORIF if surgery is indicated.

push.question: How will you reduce it?
push.expect: Regional anaesthesia, such as a Bier's block, by a trained practitioner.

push.question: How will you hold the reduction?
push.expect: Neutral wrist, three-point moulding, check X-ray, clinic within 72 hours.

push.question: Does she need surgery?
push.expect: At 65 or over, non-operative can be primary unless significant deformity or nerve compromise.

curveballs.prompt: The distal fragment is displaced volarly.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Smith's fracture: unstable; consider open reduction and plate fixation.

curveballs.prompt: After manipulation her index finger is numb and getting worse.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome: split the cast, elevate, and urgent decompression if it does not settle.

curveballs.prompt: Six weeks later she cannot extend her thumb.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Extensor pollicis longus rupture: refer to hand surgery for tendon transfer.
